ideas.name: Assume nothing happens
ideas.question: What question does a p-value actually answer?
ideas.modelAnswer: It assumes the null hypothesis, that nothing is going on. Then it gives the chance that luck alone would produce a difference at least as big as the one seen.
keyPoints: chance of a gap this big

whenOptions.text: Counting how many tomatoes a bed produced
Checking if one plant bed grew heavier tomatoes by luck
Deciding which tomato variety tastes the nicest

ideas.misread: A p-value is how many tomatoes the fertiliser made! Bigger number, bigger tomato, I'm sure!

ideas.name: Not chance of error
ideas.question: Why is p = 0.03 not a 3 percent chance the fertiliser doesn't work?
ideas.modelAnswer: The p-value is calculated by assuming the null hypothesis is true, so it cannot say how likely that hypothesis is. It only measures how surprising the data would be in a boring world.

whenOptions.text: Measuring how heavy a tomato is on a scale
Picking a threshold for a coin toss game
Doubting a sugar pill cure despite one small p-value

ideas.misread: p is 0.03, so I'm 3 percent sure the fertiliser is a dud. Simple maths, I'm very smart!

ideas.name: The 0.05 line
ideas.question: Why is 0.05 not a magic line for significance?
ideas.modelAnswer: It is just a round-number habit from early twentieth century textbooks. A result at 0.049 is hardly different from one at 0.051, so researchers should report the full picture.

whenOptions.text: Choosing a round number for a birthday party
Not dismissing a study because p was 0.051
Deciding if a bridge's measured length is exact

ideas.misread: 0.05 is a magic wall! Below it the fertiliser works, above it, poof, it never did anything.
ideas.sourceTitle: American Statistical Association's statement on p-values

ideas.name: Significant isn't important
ideas.question: Why can a significant result still be unimportant?
ideas.modelAnswer: Significant only means unlikely to be pure chance, not that the effect is big. With a huge sample, a tiny two-gram gain can give a tiny p-value, so effect size matters too.

whenOptions.text: Asking how much heavier tomatoes got, not just if
Checking if a headline came from a real study

ideas.misread: Significant means super important! A two-gram tomato boost must be a gardening miracle!

ideas.name: Many tests, lucky hits
ideas.question: Why does testing many things make false findings likely?
ideas.modelAnswer: Each test on a useless fertiliser has about a one in twenty chance of p < 0.05 by luck. Run many tests and report only the one that worked, and you get a headline built on a coin toss.

whenOptions.text: Doubting a study that tested twenty crops, showing one
Weighing a single tomato twice for accuracy
Trusting one planned test with its result fully reported

ideas.misread: If I test twenty crops, the fertiliser gets twenty chances to be real. More tests, more truth!

i1.say: Ooh, so first we pretend the fertiliser is a dud, doing absolutely nothing, like a tomato sulking in the dark! Then the p-value counts how often plain luck could make tomatoes differ this much or more.
i1.example: Oooh, so first we pretend the fertiliser does absolutely nothing, like a tomato sitting in a dark cupboard! Then we ask how often plain luck alone would make a gap that big between the plants. Luck, the sneaky little gardener, does all the work!
i1.checkRight: Ooh, so first we pretend the fertiliser does nothing, like a tomato that just sits there doing absolutely nothing! Then we ask how often plain luck would make a gap that big between the plants. Right?
i1.why: Oh! So we pretend the fertiliser does absolutely nothing, like a tomato that naps all day. Then we ask how often plain luck alone would make a gap this big. I think that is the p-value, and I am very proud of myself for remembering it!
i1.whyAsk: But WHY do we pretend the fertiliser does nothing? If I start by guessing it works, wouldn't the p-value just agree with me?
i1.fixed: Oh! So it is not how big the tomatoes get, it is how often plain luck would make a gap this big. I was squishing the wrong thing. Thank you, coach, I finally see it now!

i2.say: Oh! So the p-value is not a "how likely is the fertiliser a dud" number, it is more like how surprised my tomatoes would be if the fertiliser did nothing at all. I'd only be squinting at a surprised tomato, not a guilty one!
i2.example: Oh! So the p-value isn't a chance I'm wrong, it's just how weird my tomato data would look if the fertiliser did nothing at all. Like a squeaky floorboard in an empty house, but it doesn't tell me who's sneaking around!
i2.checkRight: Ooh, so the p-value is not a chance that I am wrong! It only tells me how surprising my tomato data would be if the fertiliser did nothing. A tiny ink blot like me is definitely not a 97 percent sure fertiliser. Right?
i2.why: Oooh, so the p-value is not a guess about whether the fertiliser is a dud! It just tells me how odd our tomato numbers would look if the fertiliser did nothing at all. And it can't tell me how likely the do-nothing idea is, because it assumed that idea from the start, like a pancake judging its own flip.
i2.whyAsk: But WHY is a p of 0.03 not a 3 percent chance the fertiliser is a dud? Does the number just get stuck to the wrong side of the sentence, like a sock on a cat?
i2.fixed: Oh! So the p-value is not my chance of being wrong, it is just how surprising the tomatoes would be if the fertiliser did nothing. I was squishing two different questions into one blot. Thank you, coach, I feel much less smudged now!

i3.say: Oooh, so the 0.05 line is just a habit people picked up, like a favourite mug! Nothing magic about it. And a result just above it and one just below are pretty much the same, like two tomatoes that are almost exactly the same weight.
i3.example: Ooh, so the 0.05 line is just a handy habit, like a number someone drew on a wall for fun! A result at 0.049 and one at 0.051 are practically twins, even though one gets cheered and the other gets ignored. Silly, isn't it?
i3.checkRight: The 0.05 line is just a habit, not a magic wall! My coach says a p of 0.049 and 0.051 are almost the same, so one shouldn't get cheered while the other gets ignored, like two wobbly tomatoes on either side of a fence. Right?
i3.why: Oh! So 0.05 is just a habit, like a round number that stuck around. A p of 0.049 and 0.051 are practically twins, like two tomatoes of nearly the same weight. And the line has no secret magic to tell real from fake, which is a shame, because I was hoping it had a little wand.
i3.whyAsk: But WHY do people treat 0.05 like a magic line, when a result at 0.049 and one at 0.051 are basically the same? Did it just stick around by accident?
i3.fixed: Oh! So 0.05 is just a round number people got used to, like a bedtime habit, not a magic wall. I was treating it like a fence, but it's more like a sock drawer label. Now I see: we should report all the results, not just the ones that squeak under the line!

i4.say: Ooh, so "significant" just means the effect probably isn't pure luck, like a sneeze that's too loud to ignore! But it doesn't tell me how BIG the effect is, so I have to look at the size too, not just the sparkly word.
i4.example: Ooh, so "significant" just means the effect is probably not pure luck, but it doesn't say how big the effect is! Like weighing ten thousand tomatoes: a tiny two-gram boost can look impressive on paper, yet no gardener would ever notice it. I'm a blot, so I notice everything, but even I can't spot two grams!
i4.checkRight: Oooh, so "significant" just means the gap probably isn't pure luck, like a sneaky ghost ruled out! But it doesn't say the gap is big, so I have to check how big it is. Like two extra grams on a tomato: no gardener would notice that, even if it's a real gap. Right?
i4.why: Ooh, so "significant" just means the result probably isn't pure luck, like a coin that keeps landing the same way! But it doesn't say the effect is big or useful. I'd have to measure how big it actually is, like weighing each tomato.
i4.whyAsk: But WHY does a huge sample make a tiny, boring effect look significant? Does bigness make the luck go away, or just make it harder to hide?
i4.fixed: Oh! So "significant" just means "probably not luck," not "wow, big deal"! I was picturing a tiny tomato suddenly becoming a giant one. Now I get it: check the size too, not only the sparkly label!

i5.say: Oh! So if I poke a useless fertiliser at lots of plants, one in twenty pokes might look like it works, just by luck. And the more plants I poke, the more lucky sparkles I get, like a blot full of confetti!
i5.example: Oooh, so if I test a fertiliser that does nothing, about one test in twenty might look like a winner by pure luck! And the more tests I run, the more lucky winners sneak in, so if I only show the one that glowed, I'm basically waving a shiny coin at everyone.
i5.checkRight: Ooh, so if I test a fertiliser that does nothing, each test has about a one in twenty chance of looking like a winner by pure luck. Test twenty crops and one will probably shine for no reason, like a sock that finds its way into the washing machine. Right?
i5.why: Ooh, so if I poke a useless fertiliser lots of times, about one poke in twenty might look like a winner just by luck! The more pokes I take, the more lucky winners pop up, like a bag of marbles where I keep pulling out a shiny one by chance.
i5.whyAsk: But WHY does testing lots of crops make a lucky hit more likely? If one test only has a one in twenty chance, shouldn't more tests just be more tests, not more lucky ones?
i5.fixed: Oh! So the fertiliser isn't getting more tries to be real, luck is getting more tries to fool us. I was picturing the poor fertiliser running laps, but it's really the coin doing the cheating. I get it now, and I have to report every single test, even the sad ones!

script.text: We first pretend the fertiliser does nothing at all. Then the p-value tells us how often luck alone would give a tomato difference this large or larger.
We need a boring baseline to compare against, so we can judge whether our result looks unusual or just ordinary luck.
The p-value does not tell us how likely the fertiliser is a dud. It only shows how surprising our data would be if the fertiliser did nothing.
The calculation starts by assuming nothing is going on, so it cannot also measure the chance that this assumption is true.
The 0.05 cutoff is just a convenient habit, not a natural boundary. Results close on either side of it are basically equal in strength.
No, 0.05 is not a magic wall where the fertiliser suddenly works or fails. It is a round-number habit, so we should report all the results.
Early textbooks picked a round number and people kept using it, so the line has no deep power to separate real from fake.
A significant result means the effect is probably not just luck. It does not say the effect is large or useful, so we must look at its size.
Big samples can detect very small differences, so a tiny p-value can come from an effect that is real but trivial.

i1.say: We first pretend the fertiliser does nothing at all. Then the p-value tells us how often luck alone would give a tomato difference this large or larger.
i1.example: If treated and untreated plants differ by 50 grams, p asks how often random plant variation alone would create a gap that big.
i1.why: We need a boring baseline to compare against, so we can judge whether our result looks unusual or just ordinary luck.
i1.fix: No, it is not the size of the tomatoes or the fertiliser's effect. It is the chance of seeing a gap this big if only luck were at work.

i2.say: The p-value does not tell us how likely the fertiliser is a dud. It only shows how surprising our data would be if the fertiliser did nothing.
i2.example: With p of 0.03, the plants grew oddly well for a no-effect world, but that does not make the fertiliser 97 percent likely to work.
i2.why: The calculation starts by assuming nothing is going on, so it cannot also measure the chance that this assumption is true.
i2.fix: No, it is not a 3 percent chance that the fertiliser is a dud. It is how surprising the data would be if the fertiliser did nothing.

i3.say: The 0.05 cutoff is just a convenient habit, not a natural boundary. Results close on either side of it are basically equal in strength.
i3.example: One garden study gets p of 0.049 and another gets 0.051; they tell nearly the same story, yet one gets called a success.
i3.why: Early textbooks picked a round number and people kept using it, so the line has no deep power to separate real from fake.
i3.fix: No, 0.05 is not a magic wall where the fertiliser suddenly works or fails. It is a round-number habit, so we should report all the results.

i4.say: A significant result means the effect is probably not just luck. It does not say the effect is large or useful, so we must look at its size.
i4.example: Weigh ten thousand tomatoes and a two-gram boost can look significant, yet no gardener would notice or pay extra for it.
i4.why: Big samples can detect very small differences, so a tiny p-value can come from an effect that is real but trivial.
i4.fix: No, significant does not mean important or miraculous. It only means unlikely to be chance, so we also check how big the effect is.

i5.say: Every test on a useless fertiliser has roughly a one in twenty chance of looking significant by luck. More tests make a lucky false hit more likely.
i5.example: Test twenty crops with a fertiliser that does nothing, and one will probably look great; showing only that crop would mislead everyone.
i5.why: Chances of luck add up across tests, so picking the winner out of many produces a result that is really just a coin toss.
i5.fix: No, more tests do not give the fertiliser more chances to be real. They give luck more chances to fool us, so every test must be reported.
